en.title: Numbers and age
en.goal: Count from 0 to 100 and say or ask someone's age.

lessons.numeros-idade: Counting to ten and saying your age

number-structure.title: How numbers work in Chinese
number-structure.body: The numbers from 0 to 10 each have their own word. From there, Chinese builds larger numbers by combining those words in a very logical way: 十一 (shí yī) is literally "ten-one" (11), 二十 (èr shí) is "two-ten" (20). It's more regular than English in this respect.

number-structure.title: 岁 (suì) — counting age
number-structure.body: To say your age, the number is followed by 岁 (suì), which works like the unit "years old" — without using the verb "to have" or "to be." The structure is: Subject + Number + 岁.

ji-vs-duo.title: 几 vs. 多 — two ways to ask "how many / how much"
ji-vs-duo.body: 几 (jǐ) is used to ask about small, expected numbers, usually up to 10. 多 (duō) before an adjective asks about degree or a larger amount, without expecting a specific small number.

ji-vs-duo.title: "Nǐ jǐ suì" or "nǐ duō dà"?
ji-vs-duo.body: Jǐ suì (几岁) is used to ask the age of children, since 几 expects a small number. For adults, the neutral and most common form is duō dà (多大) — asking an adult "jǐ suì" can sound odd.

xusui-ano-novo.title: In traditional China, your age changes at New Year — not on your birthday
xusui-ano-novo.body: In the traditional Chinese system (虚岁, xūsuì, "nominal age"), a baby is born already 1 year old, and everyone gains a year together at Chinese New Year — not on their own birthday. Today the Western system (actual age, 周岁) is the most used in daily life, but 虚岁 still appears in traditional contexts.

si-numero-azarado.title: Why the number 4 is avoided in China
si-numero-azarado.body: 四 (sì, "four") sounds very similar to 死 (sǐ, "death") — because of that similarity in sound, many people avoid the number 4 in daily life: it's common for buildings to skip the 4th floor (or apartment number), and phone numbers or license plates with a 4 can be considered less desirable. It's the same kind of superstition that the number 13 has in many Western countries.
